title: Syntax, Runtime and Logical Errors
learningObjectives: Explain syntax errors, runtime exceptions, logical defects and error isolation.

understand.concept: Syntax errors prevent Python from compiling source code. Runtime errors occur while a program executes, often as exceptions. Logical errors allow a program to run but produce an incorrect result. These categories require different investigation strategies: inspect source structure for syntax errors, trace execution and exception data for runtime failures, and compare outputs against requirements for logical defects.
understand.whyItMatters: Correctly classifying a defect helps choose the right diagnostic technique instead of treating every failure as the same kind of problem.
understand.analogy: A syntax error is an invalid instruction, a runtime error is a failed operation, and a logical error is a valid instruction that achieves the wrong goal.
understand.analogyLimit: A single defect can cause several symptoms; for example, a logical mistake may later trigger a runtime exception.
understand.summary: Syntax, Runtime and Logical Errors develops reliable debugging and software verification skills.

explain.narrative:
## Classify before fixing
A `SyntaxError` is raised when source cannot be parsed. A `NameError` or `TypeError` may occur at runtime. A logical error can be harder to detect because execution may complete normally. Tests with expected results and boundary cases are especially useful for logical defects.

You can use `compile()` to examine source text for syntax errors without executing it. For runtime errors, catch only exceptions you can handle meaningfully. For logical errors, build a minimal example and compare actual behaviour with the intended rule.
